title: Comparison of the short-term effects of Galileo training to treadmill training forward downhill on calf muscle spasticity in children with cerebral palsy
summary:
The most common accompanying symptom of the spastic calf in children with cerebral palsy is the pointed foot deformity. In everyday life, this hinders children when standing and walking. Various approaches are used to treat the spastic calf. Galileo training is already a widely used form of therapy for the treatment of children with cerebral palsy. Several studies have shown a positive effect on gait quality and muscle strength in the calf. 
Another therapeutic approach for the spastic calf is treadmill training. A specific form of treadmill training is walking forwards downhill. Treadmill training in a different form has already been investigated in studies for its effects on the muscles and walking ability of children with cerebral palsy and positive effects in terms of strength and quality of movement have been shown. However, no study has yet investigated the effect of walking forwards downhill on calf spasticity.
conditions: Cerebral palsy and other paralytic syndromes

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Diagnosis of spastic CP [unilateral, bilateral]
GMFCS Level I-III, ability to walk with or without aids Age: 7- 18 years
Sufficient cognitive capacity: Understanding of intervention instructions: Counting to 10 and performing the verbal movement task, single leg stance
Exclusion criteria:
Cardiopulmonary diseases GMFCS Level IV-V
Medication:
- Dosage change of oral baclofen within the last week
- Local botulinum toxin treatment of the calf within the last three months Surgery on the lower extremity:
- Soft tissue surgery within the last three months
- Operations with bony involvement within the last six months
- Structural contractures of the upper ankle joint: range of motion in dorsiflexion/flexion from 0° - 5° - 40°with the knee flexed
